title: The Jar of Odd Screws. A Small Museum of Problems I Meant to Fix
body: Every household has one. A jar, a tin, a drawer, the graveyard of disassembled things. Mine is a marmalade jar on the workbench shelf, currently holding two hundred and forty screws, three strange bolts I cannot identify, a washer the size of a coin, one key to nothing, and a small brass hook that has survived four moves for reasons nobody remembers. I used to see the jar as clutter. I have come to see it as an archive. Here is the museum catalog. There are the cabinet screws, uniform, dignified, collected when I replaced all the handles and could not throw away perfectly good metal. There are the flat-head strangers, probably from a lamp, possibly from a crib, definitely load-bearing in some object I no longer own. There are the self-tapping champions with their aggressive threads, the screws that bite their own path, my favorite hardware personalities. And there is the sealed envelope, taped, labeled in my late father's handwriting, which I have never opened. His jar, inherited with the workbench, had one rule. Some fasteners are a mystery on purpose. The jar turned out to be a surprisingly effective triage tool, and this is the part nobody tells you. When something in the house breaks and needs a screw, the first stop is the jar, and the jar answers one of two ways. Either it has the screw, and the repair costs nothing and takes four minutes, or it does not, and now I know the exact thing I need to buy, instead of buying an assortment kit of four hundred screws, two hundred and thirty of which will be added to the jar by future me in a gesture of perfect circular futility. The jar is also an honesty device. Every screw in it represents a moment of decision. Something came apart, and I chose to keep the hardware rather than sweep it into the bin with the packaging. That choice, multiplied over years, is the difference between a household that can fix things and one that must re-purchase them. My neighbor throws everything away in the moment and then drives to the hardware store on Saturdays with the defeated expression of a man starting from zero. My jar is not organization. It is deference. I am not deciding now. I am keeping the option alive at the cost of one drawer. There is a right way and a wrong way to run the archive, learned the hard way. The wrong way is one jar where everything meets everything, so every retrieval is archaeology. The right way is the jar plus five minutes a year. Once a year, on a rainy afternoon, the jar gets sorted. Roughly by size, honestly by feeling, into three vessels. The keepers, the probable keepers, and the jar of shame for fasteners that have sat unmoved through two annual reviews, which go to the metal recycling like soldiers finally discharged. Last month the wardrobe hinge failed and the fix came entirely from the jar, two screws, four minutes, no purchase. I stood there holding the screwdriver with an emotion I can only describe as ancestral. Somewhere my father, who kept his mysteries taped and labeled, would have said nothing and smiled. The jar does not just hold screws. It holds the household's memory of every repair it was almost ready for.
